beats.narration_text: Hi, I am Adwait Changan, and this video is about why connecting AI tools got so expensive, and the protocol built to fix it. Today we are going to learn what the Model Context Protocol actually does, which is less magical and more useful than most explanations suggest. It is a counting problem.

show.event: composer on cream; the fellow names himself and the topic

props.command: What problem does the Model Context Protocol actually solve?
output: Every app that wants every tool writes its own connector to each one.
Five apps and ten tools is fifty connectors, all maintained separately.
A protocol turns that multiplication into an addition.

beats.narration_text: The problem has a shape. Every AI app that wants to reach a tool writes code specific to that tool. Every tool that wants to be reachable gets written against separately by each app. Nobody is doing anything wrong, and the work multiplies anyway.

layers.title: Each app
layers.sub: writes code specific to every tool it wants

layers.title: Each tool
layers.sub: gets written against separately by every app

layers.title: Apps times tools
layers.sub: the connectors multiply, and each is maintained alone

props.caption: A structural cost, not a failure of anyone's engineering.

beats.narration_text: So count it. Two apps and three tools is six connectors, which is fine. Three and five is fifteen. Five apps and ten tools is fifty. Ten and twenty is two hundred. The right-hand column is the same situation with a protocol in the middle, and it grows by addition instead.

show.event: the header and small case write on
ten by twenty lands: 200 against 30, in terracotta

beats.narration_text: The effect shows up most clearly when something new arrives. Add one tool to an ecosystem of three apps and you write three connectors. With fifty apps you write fifty. Through a protocol you write one, and you write it once, no matter how many apps exist or appear later.

show.event: fifty apps completes the grid; the 1 never moves

props.caption: The right-hand number does not change. That is the property.

beats.act: ACT 3 — WHEN IT IS NOT WORTH IT
beats.narration_text: And standardising the seam does not make what crosses it good. A badly described tool is badly described in any protocol. All the connection work being solved just means the quality of your descriptions is now the thing standing between an agent and the right answer.

props.title: A Bad Tool Is Bad in Any Protocol
props.body: Solving the connection work does not improve what crosses the seam. Your descriptions become the thing standing between an agent and the right answer.

beats.narration_text: So, the verdict. Connecting apps to tools is a multiplication problem: every app writes its own connector to every tool, so five apps and ten tools is fifty pieces of work maintained separately, and ten by twenty is two hundred. A protocol standardises the seam so each side learns one shape, and the multiplication becomes an addition. Thirty instead of two hundred. Adding one new tool costs one connector instead of one per app, however many apps there are. At small scale it genuinely loses: one app and three tools is three against four. And none of this improves what crosses the seam, because a badly described tool is badly described in any protocol.

show.event: the 'at small scale it loses' line holds in terracotta

props.artifactHeading: A counting problem, not a capability
artifactLines: Apps times tools: 5 apps and 10 tools is 50 connectors, each maintained separately.
A protocol standardises the seam, so the multiplication becomes an addition: 15, not 50.
One new tool costs 1 connector instead of 1 per app — and that number never grows.
At small scale it loses. One app, three tools: direct is 3, protocol is 4.
It fixes the connection, not the content. A bad description is bad in any protocol.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here is the prompt. Count the integrations I actually have: how many applications reach how many tools, and how many separate connectors exist between them today. Then tell me what adding one more tool costs right now, and what it would cost through a shared protocol. Run that on your own stack. If the first number is already bigger than the second, the decision was made for you a while ago.

If adding one tool already costs several pieces of work, the decision was made for you.
